props.title: Split Second
props.initialSlug: Cop hunts supernatural killer in flooded future London

sections.content: Split Second emerges as a fascinating hybrid of cyberpunk noir and monster horror, starring Rutger Hauer at his gruff, post-Blade Runner (1982) best. Set in a flooded, dystopian 2008 London, it channels the grimy aesthetic of Alien (1979) while incorporating elements that would later become cyberpunk staples. The film's waterlogged metropolis predates similar environmental disasters in films like Waterworld (1995), though executed on a much tighter budget. Director Tony Maylam crafts a uniquely atmospheric thriller that, while overlooked upon release, has gained cult status for its ambitious blend of genres.

sections.content: The early 1990s saw a surge of low-to-mid-budget sci-fi horror hybrids that merged cyberpunk aesthetics with creature features. Films like Hardware (1990) and Death Machine (1994) followed similar patterns, combining future noir with monster movie DNA. These productions often featured practical effects over early CGI, resulting in tangible threats that still hold up today. Split Second particularly excels in its creature design, creating a memorable demon-like antagonist that owes as much to Predator (1987) as it does to gothic horror.

Rutger Hauer's performance as Harley Stone anchors the film firmly in the noir tradition, reminiscent of his iconic turn in Blade Runner (1982). His character's psychic connection to the monster predates similar plot devices in films like Event Horizon (1997) and adds a supernatural element that sets it apart from purely sci-fi entries. The partnership with Dick Durkin (Neil Duncan) creates a buddy cop dynamic that would be echoed in later sci-fi police films like Dark Angel (1990) and Demolition Man (1993). sections.content: The flooded London setting proves remarkably prescient, anticipating climate anxiety films like Flood (2007) and The Day After Tomorrow (2004). The production design team created a convincingly waterlogged metropolis on a limited budget, predating the more expensive but similarly themed A.I. Artificial Intelligence (2001). This environmental catastrophe backdrop adds layers of social commentary that elevate Split Second beyond simple genre exercise.
